title: SYSK Selects: How Willpower Works
summary: SYSK Selects episode in which Chuck Bryant picks the 2017 (originally February 7, 2014-era) episode "How Willpower Works" to re-listen to. The original episode covers willpower as a limited, depletable resource: Plato's higher and lower self, Robert Lamb's HowStuffWorks article, Freud's ego and ego depletion, Roy Baumeister's radish and chocolate persistence test, Baba Shiv's working memory and cake experiment, brain imaging of the prefrontal cortex during decisions, glucose as a willpower boost, the Israeli parole board study and decision fatigue (John Tierney's New York Times article), Rush's "Free Will" lyric, Dweck's work on resolve, the Stanford marshmallow experiment and a University of Rochester follow-up, and how decision fatigue may affect the poor. The episode closes with a listener mail from Todd in Oklahoma City.

Do You Suffer from Decision Fatigue?

segments.title: Selects intro and website plug
segments.summary: Chuck introduces his Selects pick, How Willpower Works, saying he needs to re-listen because he lacks willpower. Hosts mention the new website and social channels.

segments.title: Higher self, lower self, and willpower basics
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Plato's idea of a higher and lower self, and Robert Lamb's HowStuffWorks article on humans being at odds with evolved urges such as craving sugar and sex. Willpower is described as varying in amounts among people and as broader than eating or exercise.

segments.title: Willpower as a depletable meter and Freud's ego
segments.summary: Willpower is framed as a decision-making act shaped by how one views the surrounding world. Hosts compare willpower to a video-game meter that depletes and replenishes. They trace the idea to Freud's finite ego energy and its later revival.

segments.title: Baumeister radish test and Baba Shiv working memory study
segments.summary: Roy Baumeister's Florida State study found that people who resisted cookies with radishes did worse on a persistence puzzle. A University of Iowa study by Baba Shiv found that people holding a seven-digit number resisted chocolate cake less well than those holding a two-digit number.

segments.title: Brain imaging and willpower as a muscle
segments.summary: MRI studies showed the ventromedial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex lighting up during decisions, with the dorsolateral area linked to good choices. Baumeister compares willpower to a muscle. Chuck describes skipping a trip to the car for a mail key as an example of exercising willpower.

segments.title: Glucose, decision fatigue, and the Israeli parole board
segments.summary: Glucose is described as replenishing willpower, a finding first dismissed because brain energy use is steady. A study of Israeli parole decisions found that prisoners seen later in the day, away from a meal break, were much less likely to be paroled, which is attributed to risk-averse decision fatigue.

segments.title: Rush lyric, Dweck, genetics, and the marshmallow experiments
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the Rush song Free Will and its lyric about choosing not to decide. They cover Stanford and Dweck research on people who feel resolve is limited, genetic and epigenetic influences, the 1960s marshmallow test and its later life outcomes, and a University of Rochester follow-up in which kids who were promised art supplies waited longer after a promise was kept.

segments.title: Poverty and decision fatigue
segments.summary: Hosts discuss a point from the Tierney article that people in poverty face more decisions about spending and so may experience decision fatigue faster, which may compound the cycle of poverty.

segments.title: Listener mail from Todd in Oklahoma City and Wikipedia thanks
segments.summary: A listener named Todd writes that the podcast helped him impress his girlfriend with interesting facts. The hosts also thank a fan for help with the Wikipedia page, with the name pronounced in the episode.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts point listeners to the How Stuff Works article on willpower, to social channels, email, and the website.
